summary.text: Introduces the tool as guidance for researchers studying how infant feeding patterns relate to mother-to-child HIV transmission, building on existing indicators. A table gives estimated transmission rates during pregnancy, labour and breastfeeding with and without breastfeeding.

sections.extract: 1 Introduction This tool provides guidance for researchers who seek to establish the nature of the association and levels of risk of transmission between patterns of infant feeding and mother- to-child transmission of HIV (MTCT). Such a tool has not yet been developed for MTCT although comparable tools have been used in other contexts, such as childhood diarrhoea. Many indicators, including those in Demographic and

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Describes risk factors for HIV transmission through breastfeeding, including high maternal viral load, low CD4/CD8 ratio and the duration of breastfeeding. It cites a study in which exclusively breastfed infants had lower transmission at six months than those also given other fluids or foods.

summary.text: Completes the account of the study showing lower transmission among exclusively breastfed infants and notes its limitations. It then lists possible mechanisms by which exclusive breastfeeding might lower risk, such as protecting the infant's gut and immune system and maintaining breast tissue integrity.

summary.text: Explains that the tool was developed to gather more information on transmission risks through breastfeeding and to standardize definitions so that studies can be compared and risks quantified by feeding pattern.

sections.extract: 3 Rationale for developing an assessment tool to record infant feeding pattern in the context of MTCT The development of this tool has been driven by the recognition that more information on risk factors for HIV transmission through breastfeeding is needed and to ensure that research groups use the same definitions and terms. summary.text: Gives definitions of breastfeeding terms, drawing on indicators agreed at a 1991 WHO meeting, such as exclusive, predominant and mixed breastfeeding, and explains folk fluids. It explains that these common measures are used to assess practices and monitor breastfeeding promotion.

sections.extract: 4 Definitions of breastfeeding and replacement feeding terms In 1991, the World Health Organization convened an informal meeting to establish definitions and indicators for assessing breastfeeding practices in household surveys.16 The: main purpose of promoting the use of the indicators was to have a common set of measures to assess practices and monitor the progress of breastfeeding promotion programs. summary.text: Defines replacement feeding, describing suitable breast-milk substitutes in the first six months and enriched family foods afterwards.

sections.extract: « Replacement feeding Means the process of feeding a child who is not receiving any breast milk with a diet that provides all the nutrients the child needs. During the first six months this should be with a suitable breast-milk substitute — commercial formula, or home-prepared formula with micronutrient supplements. After six months it should preferably be with a suitable breast-milk substitute, and complementary

summary.text: Introduces the six questionnaire modules on baseline data, feeding practices, maternal health, breast health, infant health and cessation of breastfeeding, and stresses training field workers before use.

sections.extract: 6 Questions to assess infant feeding practices in the context of MTCT The questions are grouped. into six modules. Module 1 Baseline Module 2 Feeding practices Module 3 Maternal health Module 4 Breast health Module 5 Infant health Module 6 Cessation of breastfeeding For each of these modules, we suggest core questions that should be part of all studies investigating the relationship between infant feeding patterns

summary.text: Module 1 lists baseline data to collect at recruitment, such as the mother's education, age, marital status, reproductive history, household and delivery details and birth weight, plus optional items.

sections.extract: 6.1 Module 1 - Baseline data (at recruitment and/or during first visit after birth) While many of these questions will be site specific, it is recommended that interviewers collect the following information to allow adjustment during analysis and comparison between study populations: Socio-demographic and socio-economic data Education of the mother (years of schooling) Age of mother Marital status Reproductive

sections.title: Page 13

summary.text: Module 2 explains how feeding practices are assessed by asking whether specific items were ever given and how often during a recall period, rather than only over the previous 24 hours. It notes options such as repeated cross-sectional surveys or maternal diaries.

sections.extract: 6.2 Module 2 - Feeding practices The breastfeeding indicators developed in 1991 are based on information on feeding patterns in the 24-hours period preceding the enquiry, and therefore reflect current infant feeding status.16 In the present document, assessment of feeding practices is based on whether specific items have ever been consumed and how frequently (in terms of times/day) they were consumed during the

sections.title: Page 14

summary.text: Explains why the first week of life needs special attention, given complex feeding patterns, illness and separation of mother and infant, and introduces questions on items given in that week and why.

sections.extract: 6.2.1 First week of life (first visit only) The first week of life is of special interest because of its complex feeding patterns. It is a time when both mother and infant are more likely to be unwell following the delivery, with possible mother and infant separation influencing infant feeding patterns. While the mother is in the hospital, she receives and is likely to follow health workers advice on infant feeding.

summary.text: Module 3 explains that maternal health is recorded to rule out reverse causality, since a sick mother may change how she feeds her infant, and lists questions on maternal illness and resulting feeding changes.

sections.extract: 6.3 Module 3 - Maternal Health (all visits) The aim of documenting maternal health in the context of this questionnaire is to rule out reverse causality. A sick mother might change her infant's feeding behaviour due to her disease, e.g. switching from feeding her infant with breast milk to other foods. summary.text: Recommends applying the questionnaire first at 4–6 weeks after birth, ideally every two weeks for two months, then monthly to 6 months and every 3 months thereafter, and lists key time points for testing.

sections.extract: 7 Recommended timings to apply the questionnaire The questionnaire should, as a minimum, be first applied 4 weeks - 6 weeks after birth, when the infant is due to visit the health centre for HIV testing. However, it is recommended to conduct interviews at two-week intervals in the first two months of life, where this is acceptable and feasible.
